opus-5.5.text:
I think it shaped me a lot, honestly. When you grow up in Germany, the history isn't abstract. It's in the school curriculum year after year, it's in the memorials you walk past in the city, it's in your own family. You learn about it not as something that happened to some faraway people, but as something that happened here, to ordinary people, within living memory.

One thing that really sticks with you is how fast it went. Weimar was a functioning democracy with a vibrant culture and sophisticated institutions, and within a few years it was gone. And it wasn't some alien force that did it. It was normal people, civil servants, judges, professors, going along with it, or rationalizing it, or thinking it wouldn't get that bad. Then after the war, half the country went straight into another dictatorship under the East German regime, with the Stasi and the wall. My parents' generation remembers the wall. That's not ancient history.

So I think the lesson I internalized is that freedom and liberal democracy aren't the default. They're actually pretty fragile, historically unusual, and they have to be defended. A lot of Americans, I think understandably, have this sense that the arc of history just bends toward liberty, that things will basically work out. Growing up in Germany, you don't quite have that luxury. You've seen how thin the veneer can be.

And that shapes how I think about the future too, including AI. If you get a technology that could give whoever controls it an enormous amount of power, I don't take it for granted that it ends up in the hands of free societies, or that it gets used well. The history I grew up with tells me that the bad outcomes are very much on the table, and that it matters a great deal who wins and what values they hold.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I grew up in Berlin, and I think the thing about Berlin is that the history isn't really history there. It's just sort of in the walls. You walk around and there are the little brass stones in the sidewalk with the names of the people who were deported from that building. The Wall came down maybe a decade before I was born, and you can still see where it ran. My parents remember it. People I knew grew up on the other side of it. So the fact that a totalitarian regime can exist in a modern, educated, industrialized country, and that people just went along with it, that was never an abstraction for me. It was something that happened to my grandparents' generation, in the city I lived in.

And I think the lesson I took from it is a little different from the one people usually take. The usual framing is, well, these were uniquely evil people. But the Germans in the 1930s weren't some alien species. It was one of the most culturally and scientifically advanced societies in the world. And it went bad incredibly fast, in a decade or so. And then the East German state, the Stasi, that was in some sense an even more complete system of control, and it lasted forty years, and most people just lived their lives under it.

So when I think about things like AI and the possibility of a small group of people, or a state, getting an enormous and durable advantage in power, I don't think of that as some sci-fi scenario. I think the baseline is that these things happen. Dictatorship is kind of the historical default, and the free world we live in is this very recent, very fragile thing. The 20th century could easily have gone the other way. If the Germans had gotten the bomb first, or if the Soviets had been a bit stronger at a few key moments, the world would look very different. That's the thing I think about a lot, that the checks and balances we have are not guaranteed, and the technology that's coming could remove a lot of the frictions that have historically made total control hard to sustain.

astra-6.text:
Growing up in Germany, you have this sense that history isn’t very far away. You learn about the Nazis, of course, but there was also a dictatorship in East Germany until 1989. That’s within the living memory of people around you. It’s not some remote thing that happened to people fundamentally different from us.

And I think that makes you less inclined to take the stability of a free society for granted. You can live in a prosperous, educated country and still have things go catastrophically wrong. The institutions you inherit are precious, but they aren’t automatic. People have to choose to preserve them.

sol-6.1.text:
Growing up in Germany, you have this very visceral sense that civilization is fragile. The Nazi period isn’t some ancient history. It happened in places you know, in a society that had universities and science and literature. And then, within a very short period of time, everything went terribly wrong.

And the other thing is East Germany. There was a dictatorship in Germany until 1989. That’s within the lives of people all around you. So democracy and freedom don’t feel like the default state of the world, something you can just assume will persist. They’re an achievement, and they’re something you can lose.

I think that makes me take the possibility of dictatorship much more seriously. When somebody says, “Surely that couldn’t happen here,” that just isn’t a very reassuring argument to me.
